I don't... I don't really know if I'd say I feel hopeless, exactly? It's more just... well, everything just feels so gray. Guilty? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I definitely don't blame myself for the explosion itself, because, well, I was really just there to do my job. As an underwriter, we don't always do site visits—usually, the loss control engineers handle the actual physical inspections—but my manager has been really pushing me to get more field experience this quarter so I can move up to senior underwriter next year. So I was literally just there with my hard hat and my tablet, walking a few steps behind the facility manager, checking off boxes about their fire suppression systems and verifying the square footage against the broker's application. I didn't touch any machinery, I didn't interact with whatever equipment actually caught fire. I was just observing. 

So, no, I know I didn't cause it. It was just a horrific, freak accident. A gas leak or a mechanical failure or whatever the fire marshal's official report is eventually going to say—which, like I said, I haven't read because I can't even bring myself to look at the file. But I definitely don't feel responsible for the actual event. 

If anything, I just feel... I don't know, frustrated? Unlucky? Because, honestly, I wasn't even supposed to be the one on that account in the first place. My coworker, Dan, was the lead on that specific industrial portfolio, but his wife had to be induced early—she had preeclampsia, I think, it was a whole stressful thing, but they're both fine now, thankfully—so he went on paternity leave two weeks ahead of schedule. And because he left so suddenly, his whole queue got redistributed among the rest of the team, and that specific warehouse got dumped on my desk. 

So I was the one who had to drive out to the industrial park that Tuesday. I just happened to be standing in the wrong place at the absolute wrong time. So, yeah, no guilt about causing it, and I don't think I'm blaming myself for what happened. I just... I just keep wishing I hadn't been the one assigned to go, you know? But I know it wasn't my fault. I was just doing my job.

I don't know if I'd say sad or angry exactly, but irritable? Absolutely. It's like my fuse is just completely gone. And it's over the stupidest, smallest things that have literally nothing to do with the warehouse or the explosion or even my industrial policies. It’s like my baseline level of patience has just evaporated.

And almost instantly, my face got hot and I felt so incredibly embarrassed. Because that is just not who I am. That’s not how I usually treat people, ever. I pride myself on being approachable and a good team player at work, you know? But right now, my skin just feels so thin, like every little interruption or tiny inconvenience is this massive, grating annoyance that I just can't handle. I did go over and apologize to him later by the breakroom, and I blamed it on being stressed about a deadline, but I still feel awful about it. So, yeah, the irritability is definitely there, and it's spilling over onto people who really don't deserve it at all.

And literally from that very first night back in my own apartment, the sleep problems started. I thought maybe it was just the adrenaline at first, like when you drink too much coffee late in the day, but it’s been a full week now, and every single night is exactly the same routine of tossing and turning and jolting awake. I haven't had one single night of normal rest since the explosion.\n\nDoctor: Since the explosion, have you been feeling constantly on edge, easily startled, or overwhelmed by negative emotions like fear, sadness, or anger?\n\nPatient: Oh, God, yes. Constantly on edge doesn't even begin to cover it. It's like... it's like every nerve in my body is completely frayed and exposed. I went back into the office on Monday—which, in hindsight, was probably a terrible idea, considering I haven't slept and I feel like I'm barely holding it together—but I figured I had to try and get back to normal, right? Just sit at my desk, do my underwriting, pretend everything is fine. \n\nBut I can't. I just can't. The office is usually so quiet, you know? Just the hum of the AC and people typing. But now... every little noise feels like a physical blow. Just yesterday, the big copier down the hall jammed—it does that all the time, it makes this loud clanking noise—and I practically leaped out of my chair. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out. And then, later, one of the junior analysts came up behind me to ask a question about a policy rider, and he just said \"Hey,\" and I screamed. I actually screamed in the middle of the open-plan office. I spilled my coffee everywhere. I jumped like... like the whole building was coming down around us. \n\nAnd the worst part is, it's not just a quick jump and then I'm fine. It takes me forever to calm down. I'll sit there for, I don't know, five, ten minutes, just gripping the edge of my desk, trying to catch my breath, feeling this overwhelming sense of dread, like something terrible is about to happen again. Everyone was staring at me, and I felt so embarrassed, but I couldn't stop shaking. It's just... a door slams, someone drops a book, a phone rings too loud, and my brain instantly goes right back to that warehouse, and I just panic. I've never been a jumpy person, never, but now I feel like I'm just waiting for the next disaster to strike every single second of the day.\n\nDoctor: Since the explosion, have you noticed any changes in your mood or thoughts, such as feeling hopeless, detached from others, or having trouble experiencing positive emotions?\n\nPatient: I don't... I don't really know if I'd say I feel hopeless, exactly? It's more just... well, everything just feels so gray. Like, I don't think I'm depressed in the way people talk about being depressed, where you can't get out of bed because you're so sad, but... I just don't really feel much of anything good right now. I tried to explain it to my sister on the phone the other day. She called because we usually do this Sunday brunch thing, just the two of us, we've been doing it for years since I moved into the city. And she was going on about this new mimosa place that opened up near her apartment, and normally I'd be so excited, I love trying new places, especially with her, but I just... I couldn't even fake being interested. \n\nI ended up telling her I was too tired, which is true, obviously, with the sleep thing, but it was also just that the thought of sitting there, trying to smile and laugh and talk about normal things like bottomless brunch and work gossip... it just felt impossible. It felt like I was watching her talk from a million miles away. I feel really disconnected from everyone, to be honest. Even at work, before the whole screaming incident, people would be chatting by the water cooler about their weekends, and I just felt like an alien trying to study human behavior. I can't connect to what they're feeling. It's like my brain has just shut off the part that feels joy or excitement or even just normal contentment, and all that's left is this constant, exhausting hum of anxiety and exhaustion. So I wouldn't say hopeless, but definitely... definitely detached. I just feel really far away from the person I was a week ago.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest in activities or hobbies that you used to enjoy, or found it difficult to feel pleasure in things that would normally make you happy?\n\nPatient: I mean, it's hard to say if I've actually lost interest, because... well, it's only been exactly a week, right? And this whole past week has really just been about trying to survive the day and get through work without having a complete breakdown in front of my coworkers. \n\nNormally, I'm really active. I do this indoor cycling class, like a spin class, three times a week at this boutique studio a few blocks from my apartment. The instructor, Sarah, she's absolutely great, she always plays this amazing 90s hip-hop playlist, and usually, I look forward to it all day. It's my main stress relief after dealing with insurance policies for eight hours. But this week... I haven't gone. I canceled all my classes on the app. But I don't think it's because I've lost interest in cycling, exactly? It's more like... how could I possibly sit in a dark, enclosed room with loud, pounding music and people shouting right now? Just the thought of the bass from those heavy speakers vibrating through the floor makes my chest tight. I feel like I'd have a panic attack before the warm-up was even over.\n\nAnd my other big hobby is reading. I'm a huge reader, mostly historical fiction, which I usually do every single night before bed to wind down. I have this massive stack of hardcovers on my nightstand, and I was right in the middle of this really gripping novel about the Tudor court before the inspection. But since the sleep thing started, I haven't even opened a book. Not once. I'll pick it up, look at the cover, and then just put it right back down. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, or I'm too busy listening to every creak the building makes. \n\nSo I haven't really noticed a permanent loss of interest, if that makes sense? It's not like I look at my spin shoes or my books and think, \"I hate this now, I never want to do this again.\" It's just that right now, in this exact moment, I physically and mentally cannot bring myself to engage with any of it. I'm just too completely drained. So, yeah, I don't know if you'd count that as losing interest, or if it's just... I don't know, a temporary pause because my brain is just too full of the warehouse and the anxiety to make room for anything fun.\n\nDoctor: Since the warehouse explosion, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I mean... especially at work. Like I said, I went back to the office, and I'm an underwriter, so my whole job is assessing risk and reviewing these properties, right? And I handle a lot of commercial property, specifically industrial stuff. But the actual file for that warehouse... the one where the explosion happened? It's just sitting there in my digital queue. I'm supposed to be finalizing some of the paperwork on it, or at least organizing it for the claims department, but I haven't touched it. I physically can't. \n\nJust seeing the client's name or the property address pop up in my inbox... my stomach just completely drops. It’s this awful, heavy, sickening feeling, like I’m on a roller coaster that just went over the edge, and I literally have to click away and minimize the window before I panic. \n\nAnd the crazy thing is, it’s not even just that specific file anymore. It’s starting to bleed into everything else. Like, any calls that come in about my other industrial accounts—you know, manufacturing plants, distribution centers, anything remotely similar to that warehouse—I just sit there and stare at the caller ID on my desk phone. I let every single one of them go straight to voicemail. I know I need to answer them, I know my manager is going to pull my phone metrics at the end of the week and see that my response time is totally tanking, because usually I pride myself on clearing my queue by the end of the day. But I just... I can't do it. Even just the thought of opening an email about a standard industrial policy makes my stomach drop all over again. I'll see the subject line from a broker about a new industrial site, and I just freeze. So, I'm just avoiding all of it. I'm just letting the voicemails pile up and ignoring the emails and pretending they don't exist, which is terrible for my job, I know, but I just don't know how to force myself to look at them right now.\n\nDoctor: Have you been blaming yourself or feeling guilty about what happened during the warehouse inspection?\n\nPatient: Guilty? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I definitely don't blame myself for the explosion itself, because, well, I was really just there to do my job. As an underwriter, we don't always do site visits—usually, the loss control engineers handle the actual physical inspections—but my manager has been really pushing me to get more field experience this quarter so I can move up to senior underwriter next year. So I was literally just there with my hard hat and my tablet, walking a few steps behind the facility manager, checking off boxes about their fire suppression systems and verifying the square footage against the broker's application. I didn't touch any machinery, I didn't interact with whatever equipment actually caught fire. I was just observing. \n\nSo, no, I know I didn't cause it. It was just a horrific, freak accident. A gas leak or a mechanical failure or whatever the fire marshal's official report is eventually going to say—which, like I said, I haven't read because I can't even bring myself to look at the file. But I definitely don't feel responsible for the actual event. \n\nIf anything, I just feel... I don't know, frustrated? Unlucky? Because, honestly, I wasn't even supposed to be the one on that account in the first place. My coworker, Dan, was the lead on that specific industrial portfolio, but his wife had to be induced early—she had preeclampsia, I think, it was a whole stressful thing, but they're both fine now, thankfully—so he went on paternity leave two weeks ahead of schedule. And because he left so suddenly, his whole queue got redistributed among the rest of the team, and that specific warehouse got dumped on my desk. \n\nSo I was the one who had to drive out to the industrial park that Tuesday. I just happened to be standing in the wrong place at the absolute wrong time. So, yeah, no guilt about causing it, and I don't think I'm blaming myself for what happened. I just... I just keep wishing I hadn't been the one assigned to go, you know? But I know it wasn't my fault. I was just doing my job.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself feeling unusually sad, angry, or irritable, even when you're not thinking about the warehouse incident?\n\nPatient: I don't know if I'd say sad or angry exactly, but irritable? Absolutely. It's like my fuse is just completely gone. And it's over the stupidest, smallest things that have literally nothing to do with the warehouse or the explosion or even my industrial policies. It’s like my baseline level of patience has just evaporated. \n\nLike, just on Wednesday afternoon... there's this junior analyst on our team. He just started maybe three or four months ago, right out of college, and he's still learning the ropes of how we format our risk assessment spreadsheets for the senior team. And usually, I'm really patient with the new hires. I remember exactly how overwhelming it was when I first started out, so I try to be helpful. But he came over to my cubicle to ask a question about a formula—just a really simple, basic formatting thing on a spreadsheet that wasn't pulling the right data. \n\nAnd instead of just showing him how to fix it, like I normally would without a second thought, I just... I completely snapped at him. I mean, I practically bit his head off. It was way, way harsher than I meant to be. The whole row of desks got quiet, and the poor guy just looked like a deer in headlights, mumbled an apology, and practically ran back to his desk. \n\nAnd almost instantly, my face got hot and I felt so incredibly embarrassed. Because that is just not who I am. That’s not how I usually treat people, ever. I pride myself on being approachable and a good team player at work, you know? But right now, my skin just feels so thin, like every little interruption or tiny inconvenience is this massive, grating annoyance that I just can't handle. I did go over and apologize to him later by the breakroom, and I blamed it on being stressed about a deadline, but I still feel awful about it. So, yeah, the irritability is definitely there, and it's spilling over onto people who really don't deserve it at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling angry, guilty, or depressed specifically about the warehouse incident, even when you’re not directly reminded of it?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying before about the guilt, I definitely don't feel guilty.
